title: Build AI the Right Way: The 10 Cs
content:
A practical checklist for building smart, scalable AI applications

If you have an idea for implementing an AI solution, some kind of framework to think it through is better than none. This is a guide, not a solution.

Start by writing your idea down — just a good paragraph. It might be a feature within an existing product, like a new chatbot, or something entirely new built with an “AI-first” approach.

Once you’ve done that, go through the checklist below and write a sentence or short paragraph for each point — or simply think each one through. By the end, you should have a solid starting point for your project and a clearer understanding of its complexities (or, ideally, the lack of them!).

Bonus — you can also talk to a GPT about your ideas here https://chatgpt.com/g/g-6862e9552d408191b26b5fee7d5498ab-the-10cs-build-ai-the-right-way that has knowledge of the 10Cs

1. Common Sense 🧱

Do we actually need AI for this?

Seems obvious, but first, think through your use case. The AI hype is infectious — granted — but what is it specifically that AI (be it LLM, GenAI, custom model, etc.) is doing that can’t be done using low-effort solutions? Maybe something already exists — an open-source project or a no-code solution — that works perfectly for this problem. Sense-check it first, because otherwise you’re going to have to work out the other 9 Cs!

TL;DR: If you can solve it with simple logic, filters, rules off the shelf technology — do that first. Use AI where it truly adds value.

  • Outline the non-AI version of the solution
  • Identify what AI adds that rules can’t
  • Justify the added complexity and cost

2. Context 📍

What data do we have? What do we need?

When your idea is running, what information does it need — and when does it need it? Context is king if you’re going to figure out how to get your solution working. Do a sense check of the available information: does it exist in an easily accessible source, either via a low-tech solution or something a developer can wire up? The more complex the context, the harder it might be to source. And remember — context is also linked to performance: fetch what you need, no more.

TL;DR: Know what info you’re starting with and what you need to collect before asking the AI anything

  • Current user state, session data, system context
  • Required inputs before AI processing
  • Data collection strategy

3. Complexity 🎯

How sophisticated should the AI response be?

At this point, if you haven’t already, write down what you want the AI to return — just a paragraph. Then, if you’re brave, try distilling it into a single sentence: “Return a response to help a person X with query Y.” The harder it is to distil the response, the more complicated the solution is likely to be. Think carefully about the required output. If it’s not text or a summary — if it’s code, for example — consider exactly what needs to be returned and why.

TL;DR: Match the AI’s thinking power to the actual problem — don’t use a sledgehammer for a thumbtack

  • Simple lookup vs. reasoning vs. generation
  • Input complexity → output complexity matching
  • Processing requirements alignment

4. Capacity ⚡

Can both the AI and your system handle the workload?

If you have high complexity and a large amount of context, capacity probably won’t be your friend. In these cases, think about how often you need to request information. Does it need to be live? Maybe the solution doesn’t require real-time responses. If it does, how many users might be making requests at the same time? The choice of model, services used, where they’re hosted, and how the solution is designed all feed into one key number: how many concurrent users will you need to support?

TL;DR: AI models have limits, but so do your servers — plan for both bottlenecks

  • AI token limits and input constraints
  • Your infrastructure scaling capacity
  • Response time requirements
  • Throughput and concurrent request handling

5. Concise ✂️

How can we minimize overhead?

Now you’ve thought about capacity — never an easy one to estimate — it’s time to think about reducing complexity. This is where smart prompt, model, or system design comes in. Ask yourself: what can be done to reduce bandwidth while still achieving the desired outcome? Can your prompts be more concise? Can you offload pre-processing or post-processing outside the model? Maybe you can cache results or batch requests. Smaller context windows, trimmed inputs, and smarter use of tools or APIs can make a huge difference. Reducing complexity isn’t just about performance — it’s about making your solution scalable and sustainable from day one.

TL;DR: Shorter prompts = faster responses. Be direct and specific about what you want

  • Streamlined prompts, clear constraints
  • Structured output formats
  • Remove unnecessary context

6. Confidence 🛡️

What happens when AI fails?

Is the AI business-critical? What happens if it fails? The impact depends on the use case, so think it through. AI solutions rely on models — hosted either in-house or by third parties — and these services will go down occasionally. Not often, but enough to matter. So, what’s your plan? Can you fall back to cached responses? Is there an offline or simplified version of the solution? Think about graceful degradation and map out your failovers. If the AI vanishes for a moment, your product shouldn’t fall apart with it.

TL;DR: AI will mess up sometimes — have a backup plan ready

  • Error detection and handling
  • Fallback mechanisms
  • Confidence scoring and thresholds

7. Control 🎚️

How constrained should responses be?

Now you’ve planned your fancy AI service — what exactly will it return? If you’re using an LLM, you can ask it nicely to give you X, Y, and Z, but there might be grey areas — especially around how you want Z to be formatted. Think about how fine-grained the responses need to be. Do you need structured output? Markdown? JSON? Bullet points? The clearer you are, the easier it is to integrate into the rest of your product. Make sure the format and fidelity of the response align with the overall experience you’re building.

TL;DR: Be clear about what kind of answer you want — creative ideas or strict formats

  • Output format specifications
  • Creative boundaries and guidelines
  • Response validation rules

8. Continuity 🔗

Does context need to persist?

Most AI tools don’t have default memory — that’s a product decision on your side. Do you need to persist conversations, previous changes, or user state? Or is the use case a one-and-done interaction? Memory adds engineering overhead, so be deliberate. If memory is needed, ask: how much, for how long, and for what purpose? Are you storing full conversations, summaries, key actions? Define this early — your architecture (and data privacy model) depends on it.

TL;DR: If your task spans multiple steps, make sure the AI can “remember” what happened before

  • Session management strategy
  • State preservation across interactions
  • Context summarization approach

9. Cost 💰

Is the value worth the expense?

Now you’ve sussed out some of the core issues — do you know how much it’ll cost? That could be API fees, infrastructure, or the ROI on engineering time. But cost isn’t just dollars. Think about the net benefit: does it genuinely improve the user experience? Will it attract X more users? Will it generate data that’s useful for future model training? And don’t ignore the hidden costs — like time spent on research, opportunity cost, or delaying other features. Every AI feature has a price tag, even if it’s not on the invoice.

TL;DR: Fancy AI calls cost money — save them for features that actually matter

  • Token usage optimization
  • Caching and batching opportunities
  • ROI on AI processing

10. Compliance ⚖️

Are we meeting legal and ethical standards?

Want to send up a ton of PII just to get the idea working? Probably not your best move — unless you’ve got strong anonymisation in place or you’re running a locked-down, self-hosted model. Think about your industry’s regulatory landscape. In EdTech, for example, you’re dealing with sensitive data and often with minors. Who’s the demographic this feature touches? Do your privacy policies or T&Cs need an update? And yes… is the concept even ethical? (Yeah, we know — this bit isn’t fun, but it’s probably the most important downstream.)

TL;DR: Don’t get sued, don’t be creepy, handle user data responsibly

  • Data privacy and consent
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Bias and safety considerations

Use this checklist during design reviews and before shipping AI features.

title: I Created a “Zen” productivity GPT… here’s what I learned
content:
Am I a productivity expert?

No. I had been looking for an excuse to create a GPT using ChatGPT “Create a GPT” editor. I naturally floundered around trying to think of an idea for an actually half useful GPT. Being a software engineer I have been leaning on GPT and GitHub co-pilot a fair bit, maybe there was something I could do there? I mean it would make sense to create a GPT based on my own sphere of knowledge… or would it?

Naturally I landed on building a productivity assistant. Now I have some intuitive knowledge of productivity, having been relatively productive my adult working life, but I couldn’t say I’m a productivity expert. This raises the first question, before digging into creating such a productivity tool, does having a shallow grasp of a problem space mean I can’t create an effective GPT in that space? Is it enough that I transfer my intent and hope for the best, in this case that ChatGPT has enough self-help and productivity documentation baked into the training data that it could be an effective tool?

This is an interesting thought, because now that the ability to create these GPT’s is out there, you should question how deep the creators knowledge is versus the heavy lifting (or hallucinating!) that the model is doing. Anyway, I digress…

Let’s just build it

I’ve been very impressed with the speed at which OpenAI has released update after update. For, what I imagine, is becoming a relatively monolithic software company they do know how to churn out features.

First off, you can find useful instructions for how to build a GPT here: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554397-creating-a-gpt They are simple, but feel free to follow me if you want…

Steps

  • Login to https://chat.openai.com/
  • Click the “Explore” option on the left (desktop)
  • Click “Create a GPT”
  • Think of name of a GPT (and an idea!) In my case I thought of “Zen” on the fly and then Googled what Zen actually means (don’t want to look too stupid)
Japanese school of Mahayana Buddhism emphasizing the value of meditation and intuition rather than ritual worship or study of scriptures
  • So, it sounds good at least…
  • I also created the logo in a separate chat window… mistake! Looking at the screenshot above you can see that if you click the “+” you can upload your own photo or “Use DALL-E”.
  • I filled in the name, gave the GPT a description. I worked out that keeping the description short works best because it appears underneath the GPT logo.
  • I gave the GPT instructions using the “Act as…” style prompt with “## Directives” as bullets and “## Output” bullets to describe style of outputs.
  • Conversation starters threw me (I needed another coffee I think). These are the quick links above the input box (see below) NOT for the GPT to start a conversation with you (although that might be a useful feature if you’re reading OpenAI…)
  • There you can toggle if you want to embed files, which I believe are contextual knowledge you can give the GPT. I did have a look for open source self help, but didn’t have much time in my half hour window…
  • There are options to enable capabilities “Web browsing”, “Dall-E Image Generation”, “Code Interpreter”. I clicked all three. Edit — Clicking any of these will make the GPT only consumable by pro users (as these are pro features!) so I opted to edit my prompt a little and turn these off… This wasn’t all that clear in the editor. Edit — Ok I assumed turning them off would make it accessible by non pro users, apparently this isn’t the case: https://community.openai.com/t/cannot-share-a-gpt-with-people-who-dont-have-a-pro-plan/502997 shame…
  • I used the “Preview” window on the right to test it out and was incredibly impressed with how quickly, with a few tweaks it pretty much worked how I expected.
  • You can publish from the top right menu as well as edit how the GPT is displayed e.g. with or without your name and whether you have a domain (I don’t!)
  • One thought, there is no option to choose which version of GPT you are using, so when you are in “Preview” which version are you talking with at any moment? I know there is plenty of evidence out there about the variable qualities of models, certainly for different problem, I wonder how and when OpenAI choose these? And when you test should you know and then be update when the model changes so you can re-test?

Publishing and Testing ?

I wonder how thorough people will be testing these? I was able to create my Zen productivity tool, wasn’t required to even test it, and published it to the general public in less than an hour. The way this works and how quickly I was able to do this, based on what we had just over a year ago is impressive! But it feels like the quality could get a little diluted?

Link to a couple of test conversations below:
- https://chat.openai.com/share/202a534b-7a04-4244-b8d2-fdc3b0b784be
- https://chat.openai.com/share/821e0161-bbd2-4953-9a9b-2d3f338f0152

So I’m all done?! Here’s a link to the final version: https://chat.openai.com/g/g-GIofveU3s-zen-productivity

Let me know if you have any thoughts, share you conversations and let me know if you’ve also managed to create some cool GPT’s.

title: Saying hello to Microsoft Semantic Kernel V1
content:
(and upgrading from preview)

TL;DR

Microsoft have recently announced that Semantic Kernel (effectively a Microsoft equivalent of LangChain for martialling LLM’s) is out of preview and into a new V1 release.

Semantic Kernel is designed to build agents that can call your existing code. It is available for C#, Python and Java and provide an extensible and configurable way to create agents that can automate processes across different application domains.

I’ve been playing around with Semantic Kernel during the preview releases and am really excited to upgrade and try out it capabilities in our applications. As a software engineer for an EdTech start-up it’s really exciting to think about the possibilities. I’ve also got a few tips for upgrading for any of those moving over from preview.

Upgrading boiler plate for C#

I like to inject a copy of the Kernel into my application on start-up or have a utility class to initialise a new version. The old way of doing this in the preview release looked like this (abridged code):

var kernel = Kernel.Builder
  .WithLogger(provider.GetRequiredService>())
  .Build();

kernel.ImportSkill(new TextMemorySkill());

kernel.Config.AddOpenAITextCompletionService(TextCompletionModel, ApiKey);
kernel.Config.AddOpenAIChatCompletionService(ChatCompletionModel, ApiKey);

return (Kernel)kernel;

In the V1 release you declare the services attached to the Kernel in advance. You can also still attach services afterwards AFAIK, but haven’t tried this :-p

var kernelBuilder = Kernel.CreateBuilder();
kernelBuilder.Services.AddLogging(configure => configure.AddConsole());
kernelBuilder.Services.AddLogging(configure => configure.AddDebug());

kernelBuilder
    .AddOpenAIChatCompletion(TextCompletionModel, ApiKey)
    .AddOpenAIChatCompletion(ChatCompletionModel, ApiKey);

return kernelBuilder.Build();

Chat classes have been tidied up

Previously the roles e.g. System, User, Assistant where in the ChatHistory.AuthorRoles.System constant. They are now simplified to AuthorRole.System enum.

How the chat is defined has changed, as noted below. It’s subtle, but it took me a while to figure out the new classes (some of the online docs are a bit out of date and it’s so new it’s hard to Google!) In the below example you are asynchronously (perhaps via SignalR) appending the streaming content from the LLM service, in this case the OpenAI ChatGPT services.

// Old simplified example
var chatSettings = new ChatRequestSettings()
{
    MaxTokens = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.MaxTokens,
    Temperature = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.Temperature,
    FrequencyPenalty = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.FrequencyPenalty,
    PresencePenalty = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.PresencePenalty,
    TopP = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.TopP
}

var chatCompletition = semanticKernelService
  .SemanticKernel
  .GetService();

var chatHistory = (OpenAIChatHistory)chatCompletition.CreateNewChat(prompt);

var sb = new StringBuilder();

await foreach (var text in chatCompletion
  .GenerateMessageStreamAsync(chatHistory, chatSettings, cancellationToken))
{
    if (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        break;

    sb.Append(text);
}

// New simplified example
var chatSettings = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings()
{
    MaxTokens = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.MaxTokens,
    Temperature = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.Temperature,
    FrequencyPenalty = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.FrequencyPenalty,
    PresencePenalty = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.PresencePenalty,
    TopP = applicationSettings.OpenAISettings.TopP
};

var chatCompletition = semanticKernelService
  .SemanticKernel
  .GetRequiredService();

var chatHistory= new ChatHistory();

var sb = new StringBuilder();

await foreach (var text in _chatCompletion
  .GetStreamingChatMessageContentsAsync(chatHistory, 
    chatSettings, 
    cancellationToken: cancellationToken))
{
    if (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        break;

    sb.Append(text);
}

Skills are now “Plugins”

What was previously labelled as Skills are now Plugins. A plugin is a function intended (in most cases…ideally!) to hold a single responsibility e.g. Multiply two numbers or download a file from blob storage.

I’ve mostly used “native” plugins, which is another way of saying a plugin that is declare in C# (or you language of choice) in the project. The Semantic Kernel SDK has updated how these are declared from the preview version. I’ll do a TL;DR code example of the differences below for C#:

// Old example of a native function
[SKFunction("Multiply two numbers together")]
public static string MultiplyTwoNumbers(string input, SKContext context)
{
  // Few issues here like checking context prop exists etc... but anyway...
  return $"{int.Parse(context["num1"]) * int.Parse(context["num2"])}"
}

// New example
[KernelFunction, Description("Multiply two numbers together")]
public static int MultiplyTwoNumbers(
    [Description("The first number")] int number1,
    [Description("The second number")] int number2
)
{
    return number1 * number2;
}

// New example of calling this via the updated Kernel
var answer = await kernel.InvokeAsync(
"MathPlugin", "MultiplyTwoNumbers",
    new() {
        { "number1", 12 },
        { "number2", 5 }
    }
);

Note the attribute descriptions for the function and the parameters. These can be read by the calling agents to give them contextual knowledge for all the available plugins defined in the Kernel.

More updates…

There are lots of subtle changes to the SDK, I’ll be curious to hear about any annoying or particularly useful ones.
In future posts I will hopefully look into using handlebars scripts and yaml to create functions / plugins and dig further into using semantic embeddings and RAG techniques. In mean time here are some links to some useful resources for upgrading to V1:

  • Say hello to Semantic Kernel V1.0.1 | Semantic Kernel (microsoft.com)
  • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/semantic-kernel/agents/plugins/using-the-kernelfunction-decorator?tabs=Csharp
  • GitHub — BLaZeKiLL/semantic-kernel-v1.0-hackathon: Come hack with the Semantic Kernel v1.0 SDK!
  • Migrating from the Sequential and Stepwise planners to the new Handlebars and Stepwise planner | Semantic Kernel (microsoft.com)
  • semantic-kernel-starters/sk-csharp-hello-world at main · microsoft/semantic-kernel-starters · GitHub

title: Leveraging AI in EdTech: A Year in Review and Future Outlook
content:
In the past year at our EdTech start-up, researching how we could integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT has been an eye-opening experience. Our platform, designed for teachers, students, and parents, already featured a chat-based system. The possibilities for how and where we can integrate LLMs are exciting but not without issues.

We’d been exploring new UX designs for a while, and our chat-based system with real-time tutor support was already in place. The user adoption of ChatGPT was a pleasant surprise, confirming we were on the right track. But how could we effectively implement LLMs to help our business scale and how to improve the user experience?

Experimenting with AI in Education

We’re pushing boundaries with how we can potentially implement AI-augmented tutoring (we aren’t there yet!). Using LLM models in student conversations has its challenges, especially in math, but it’s an exciting frontier. We’re experimenting with Python and even considering third-party APIs like Wolfram Alpha to boost GPT’s accuracy and functionality.

Our content team is using AI to generate educational material, frame engaging questions, and add real-world contexts. It’s a significant leap from a year ago when such AI applications were nearly unimaginable.

AI Tools for Developers

On a personal note, as a software engineer, embracing tools like GitHub Co-pilot has changed my workflow, especially with languages I’m less familiar with.

The Future of AI in EdTech

Looking forward, the AI landscape in EdTech is buzzing with potential:

  • AI-generated educational content and user interfaces are big on our radar.
  • We’re curious about AI’s evolving role in the workforce and its impact on job roles.
  • AI in user interface design, especially for non-tech savvy users, remains a key focus.

As we look to the future, one aspect of AI technology demands special attention: AI agents. These sophisticated algorithms are set to revolutionize the way we interact with digital platforms and could play a pivotal role in the EdTech landscape.

AI Agents — Game changer?

AI agents, equipped with the ability to learn and adapt, promise to bring a new level of personalization and efficiency. They could act as virtual teaching assistants, providing real-time, tailored support to students, or even function as administrative aids, streamlining the workload for educators.

Moreover, their potential to analyse vast amounts of educational data could lead to ground-breaking insights into learning patterns, helping to refine educational strategies and personalize learning experiences further.

As we continue to explore the integration of AI into our platform, keeping a close eye on the evolution of AI agents will be crucial. Their development could unlock new capabilities and methodologies in education, making our journey into the world of AI even more thrilling.

The next few years are poised to be transformative, and AI agents will undoubtedly be at the forefront of this change. Their impact could redefine the educational experience, making it more engaging, effective, and accessible than ever before.

title: Microsoft SQL Server “Black box”
content:
TL;DR — You can use Query Store to identify poor performing queries quickly and easily! In SSMS open “Query Store” and run some of the queries and play around! Note — it does have some performance impact on production servers!

SQL server 2016+ has a great feature known as “Query Store” that acts effectively as a black box for SQL performance over a limited time frame. The default is typically 1 hour, which may seem limiting, but the black box records a ton of valuable information.

If you want to check what your Query Store settings are (or you don’t see it like in the above screenshot) you can right click your database > Properties > Query Store to check the settings. These include the data retention period.

Investigate those reports

The most useful one IMHO is the “Top Resource Consuming Queries” report. You can double click on this in the “Query Store” and wait a few moments for the report to generate. You should see something like the below screen shot.

Whoa?! You can see we have found some juicy queries to optimise. You can see the query execution plan, the query as well as other options for how to filter and view the results. For me it’s most useful to view the actual query and find in our codebase exactly where the culprit is and identify how it can be improved.

There are a load of useful diagnostics and insights you can glean from this tool. For example it will highlight missing indexes in the plan output when you drill into the queries:

Note that in the above there is also an impact rating of missing indexes. This is helpful if you have a load of pending optimisations and you want to triage them.

Resources

  • Tune nonclustered indexes with missing index suggestions - SQL Server
  • Monitor performance by using the Query Store - SQL Server

Microsoft SQL Server “Black box” was originally published in DevOps.dev on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
